note.explanation: A system is the part of a change that we are studying. Everything outside it is the surrounding. Energy moving into the system makes the change endothermic; energy moving out of the system makes it exothermic.
examples: When water boils in a beaker, the water is the system and the beaker and burner are part of the surrounding.
If a reaction releases heat to its surroundings, it is exothermic and has a negative enthalpy change.
note.checkAnswer: Boiling water is endothermic: heat energy moves from the surroundings into the water system.
note.simple: The system is the part we are looking at. The surroundings are everything else. Heat going in means endothermic; heat going out means exothermic.

note.title: System, Surroundings and Energy Transfer
steps: Identify the part being studied: this is the system.
Identify everything outside it: this is the surrounding.
If energy moves from the surrounding to the system, label the change endothermic and give it a positive sign.
If energy moves from the system to the surrounding, label the change exothermic and give it a negative sign.
note.answer: Heat energy moves from the surroundings into the water system; the change is endothermic.

rationales: Correct: the water is the part being studied, so it is the system.

rationales: Correct: in an endothermic change, energy moves from the surrounding into the system.
Incorrect: energy moving from the system to the surrounding describes an exothermic change.
Incorrect: an endothermic change involves energy transfer into the system.
Incorrect: this describes energy leaving the system, so it is exothermic.

rationales: Incorrect: the negative sign is used when energy moves from the system to the surrounding.
Correct: energy entering the system makes the enthalpy change positive.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes an exothermic change?
rationales: Correct: an exothermic change transfers energy from the system to the surrounding.

Incorrect: stopping a change is not the definition of an exothermic change.

mcqs.stem: According to the section, what is enthalpy (H), or heat content?
rationales: Correct: enthalpy is defined as the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound.
Incorrect: this describes amount of substance, not enthalpy.
Incorrect: enthalpy refers to a compound's thermal energy, not just the surrounding's temperature.
Incorrect: the energy needed to start a reaction is not the definition of enthalpy.

written.text: What is the difference between enthalpy and enthalpy change?
written.finalAnswer: Enthalpy (H) is the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound. Enthalpy change is the change in the system's enthalpy when energy is transferred during a change or reaction; it is positive when energy enters the system and negative when energy leaves it.

written.finalAnswer: Energy is needed to break a bond. Therefore, energy is absorbed by the system, so bond breaking is endothermic.

written.text:
Physical changes which usually occur around us are given in the table. Write down whether they are exothermic or endothermic.

| Physical change | Exothermic or Endothermic | Physical change | Exothermic or Endothermic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conversion of hydrated salt into anhydrous salt |  | Conduction of electricity by metals |  |
| Burning of paper |  | Dissolving ammonium chloride in water |  |
| Vapourizing liquid nitrogen |  | Formation of rain from clouds |  |
| Evaporation of dry ice |  | Dissolving sodium carbonate in water |  |
written.finalAnswer: Conversion of hydrated salt into anhydrous salt — endothermic; conduction of electricity by metals — neither exothermic nor endothermic; burning of paper — exothermic; dissolving ammonium chloride in water — endothermic; vapourizing liquid nitrogen — endothermic; formation of rain from clouds — exothermic; evaporation of dry ice — endothermic; dissolving sodium carbonate in water — exothermic.

written.text: Explain the difference between the terms heat and enthalpy.
written.finalAnswer: Heat is energy transferred from one body or system to another because of a temperature difference. Enthalpy (H) is the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound. Heat is transferred, while enthalpy describes the thermal energy content of the system.

example.question: When water is boiled in a beaker, identify the system and surrounding. State the direction of energy transfer and whether the change is endothermic or exothermic.
example.answer: The water is the system; the beaker and burner are part of the surrounding. Heat energy moves from the surrounding into the system, so the change is endothermic and positive.

explain.title: The system and its surrounding
explain.body: In Chemistry, any physical or chemical change under study may also be called a system. The chemical reaction includes reactants, products, catalyst, solvent and anything else which is important to study this reaction. Everything else which does not fall in this system is called the surrounding. In the beaker example, the water is the system and the beaker and burner are in the surrounding.

explain.title: Energy entering or leaving
explain.body: When energy is transferred from surrounding to the system, the change is called endothermic and it has a positive sign. When energy is transferred from system to surrounding, the change is called exothermic and it carries a negative sign. The surroundings get cooler when they supply energy and warmer when they receive energy.

explain.title: Enthalpy and heat
explain.body: Enthalpy (H) or heat content, is defined as the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound. The unit of its measurement is kJ mol⁻¹. Energy absorbed during a reaction increases the total enthalpy of the system; energy evolved during a reaction decreases it.

mistakes: Do not call everything in the experiment the system; the system is the part or change being studied.
Do not reverse the direction: endothermic energy goes from the surrounding into the system.
Do not give a negative sign to an endothermic change; it is positive. Exothermic change is negative.
Do not treat heat and enthalpy as identical: heat is transferred energy, while enthalpy is thermal energy stored in a compound.
When describing a beaker example, do not name the beaker or burner as the water system; they are part of the surrounding.
